written.prompt: What do the two letters reveal about the strengths and limitations of Lencho’s faith?
written.answer: The first letter shows that faith gives Lencho hope after his crop has been ruined. He makes a definite request for the money needed to sow again and survive until harvest. His second letter shows the same confidence in God, but also a limitation in his reasoning. Because he assumes God must have sent everything, he blames innocent workers for the missing sum. ଦୁଇ ଚିଠିର ପ୍ରମାଣକୁ ଏକାଠି ବିଚାର କରନ୍ତୁ।

alternatives.prompt: How does the writer develop an argument from an accident to a shared responsibility?
alternatives.answer: An industrial disaster first shows how dangerous contaminated air can be. The writer then describes less visible exposure in ordinary life, links it with factories and traffic and traces damage to people, plants, water and buildings. Possible controls follow the account of damage. The movement of pollutants across frontiers finally explains why research, spending and cooperation all matter.

written.prompt: Explain the role of light and colour in the poem about creation.
written.answer: Colour appears first in the small opening flower. The scene then expands to a mountain top coloured by the setting sun and to a sky brightened at different times of day. The trees and meadows add familiar shades closer to human activity. These visible details prepare the last stanza: eyes allow people to see such things, and lips can express appreciation of their maker. ଶେଷର eyes ସହିତ ଆଗର ଦୃଶ୍ୟ ଯୋଡ଼ନ୍ତୁ।

alternatives.prompt: How do the details of a wedding make the daughter’s decision more striking?

Yet the girl thinks of flowers, streams and fairy voices instead. She hears the possibility of sorrow beneath the songs of family happiness. The decision matters because she turns from a future visibly prepared for her.

written.prompt: Write an essay in about 200 words on “Leisure as a Part of Education”.
written.answer:
Leisure as a Part of Education
The hours after lessons or work can appear unimportant because nobody has set a task for them. Yet the school farewell address treats leisure as one of the ways in which a person’s future is formed. A pupil who learns how to use free time has already gained a useful habit.

A good book is one possibility. It allows the reader to keep learning when a teacher is no longer present. A hobby offers another kind of occupation and can provide the recreation needed for health. A companion can make such hours better or worse. A friend who encourages thoughtful choices has an influence that extends beyond a single afternoon.

This does not mean that every leisure hour must feel like another class. The speaker values recreation because people need a sound body as well as a sound mind. The important question is what an activity does to our habits. Gambling encourages a person to seek gain at somebody else’s expense. Reading, a useful interest and good company can instead give lasting satisfaction.

School will eventually end for every pupil. Free time will remain. Learning to use it well can therefore carry one part of education far beyond the school gate.

alternatives.prompt: Write an essay in about 200 words on “An Ending That Changes a Story”.
alternatives.answer:
An Ending That Changes a Story
An ending can make a reader reconsider a scene that seemed clear a moment earlier. When Grandfather returns to the zoo, he approaches the cage where he left Timothy. His confidence is understandable because he discovered the tiger as a cub and watched it grow up in his home.

The animal in the cage allows him to touch its head and even licks his hand. A leopard in the next cage frightens it. Grandfather’s attention goes immediately to the animal’s comfort, and he asks that it be moved. Anyone who has followed the history of the cub can easily accept this as a meeting between old companions.

A keeper then explains that Timothy died of pneumonia two months earlier. The tiger in the cage was captured in the hills and is considered dangerous. Suddenly the animal’s behaviour takes on a different meaning. It had not been greeting a familiar friend. Grandfather has been closer to danger than he realised.

The surprise works because the earlier details remain true. The cage was familiar, the animal did respond and Grandfather really did care. What changes is the meaning he and the reader gave those details. A single piece of information transforms the whole encounter.
alternatives.title: A Tiger in the House

alternatives.prompt: Write an essay in about 200 words on “Learning from Experience”.
alternatives.answer:
Learning from Experience
A large grain of corn puzzles everyone who sees it. Its journey from children in a ravine to a king’s possession could have ended with its being kept as an interesting object. Instead, the king wants to know where and when grain of such a size grew.

The wise men first try to solve the puzzle themselves. A hen helps reveal that the object is indeed a grain, but their books cannot tell them its history. They recognise the limits of their knowledge and suggest questioning the peasants. The first man remembers no grain like it. His father remembers larger grain than people see now but cannot identify the king’s specimen. The eldest man finally recognises it from the days when he grew and ate such corn.

Each answer is valuable, even when it admits uncertainty. It leads the king closer to the person with direct experience. The oldest man also explains what labour, land and sharing meant in his youth. At that point the object becomes more than a curiosity.

The story asks the reader to value knowledge gained through work and memory. Books begin the inquiry, but listening carefully to different generations gives the king the answer he came to seek.
alternatives.title: A Grain as Big as a Hen’s Egg

written.prompt: Write a letter of about 100 words telling a friend which voice in “Village Song” you found easier to understand and why.
written.answer:
Balasore
20 November
Dear Asha,
At first I understood the mother more easily. The clothes and cakes make it clear that many people are already preparing for the wedding. Then I read the daughter’s replies aloud. She hears water and birds where her mother hears songs of marriage and family life. I began to see why repeating the same invitation could never settle their disagreement. The girl is attracted to a different future. I still feel the mother’s anxiety, but I would now listen to the girl before asking her to stay. Which voice do you understand better?
Yours,
Mina

Her partner suggested writing two lists: facts that affected the dispute and feelings that belonged to the judge. When she compared the lists, she saw that being a friend did not alter the facts. In the next scene the two pupils exchanged roles. Each now understood why listening could be harder than announcing a decision.

What roles did the pupils receive?
